headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Special Bed Making
headings.content: Special bed making is a fundamental nursing procedure tailored to meet the specific therapeutic, diagnostic, or comfort needs of hospitalized patients in Nigerian healthcare facilities. Unlike a standard unoccupied or occupied bed, special beds are adapted for patients with distinct medical conditions such as recent surgery, cardiac distress, or acute trauma. The primary principles of special bed making revolve around patient comfort, safety, infection prevention, and therapeutic positioning. Nurses must ensure that the bed is smooth, firm, and free of wrinkles to prevent pressure ulcers, which are a major complication of immobility. Furthermore, maintaining proper body mechanics during the procedure protects the nurse from musculoskeletal strain. A well-made special bed also promotes psychological reassurance for the patient and their relatives, reflecting the high standard of holistic nursing care. Understanding the indications and specific variations of these beds is crucial for nursing students preparing for professional licensing examinations and clinical practice across diverse healthcare settings.

headings.title: General Equipment and Infection Control in Bed Making
headings.content: Effective infection control during bed making is paramount to prevent the transmission of nosocomial pathogens within the ward environment. Nurses must gather all necessary equipment beforehand, which typically includes a mattress protector, bottom sheet, draw sheet, top sheet, blanket, spread, and pillowcases. Standard precautions dictate the use of clean gloves, particularly if the linen is soiled with body fluids. A critical rule in infection control is never to shake used linen in the air, as this disperses dust, skin flakes, and microorganisms into the environment where they can be inhaled by patients or staff or settle on other surfaces. Instead, linen should be rolled tightly inward toward the center and placed directly into a laundry hamper or moisture-proof bag. Soiled linen must be held away from the nurse's uniform to prevent cross-contamination. Hand hygiene must be performed before handling clean linen and immediately after removing gloves following the disposal of dirty linen. Adhering to these protocols safeguards both the vulnerable hospitalized population and the healthcare workforce in Nigerian hospitals.

headings.title: Admission Bed
headings.content: The admission bed, also known as an intake or unoccupied opening bed, is prepared specifically to receive a newly admitted patient from the emergency department, outpatient clinic, or transfer. The primary goal of an admission bed is to welcome the patient, facilitate a smooth and comfortable transfer from a wheelchair or stretcher, and provide immediate access for any urgent initial assessments such as vital signs. The top covers of the admission bed—including the top sheet, blanket, and spread—are typically folded back in a specific manner, such as being fan-folded to the foot of the bed, folded to the side opposite the entrance, or made into a triangular apex. This configuration allows the patient to get into bed quickly without having to untuck heavy layers of linen. Equipment such as an admission pack, kidney basin, drinking water, and extra pillows may be arranged neatly nearby. For patients arriving with specific needs, waterproof pads or draw sheets are positioned correctly. The admission bed sets the tone for the patient's hospital stay, demonstrating preparedness, professionalism, and attentive nursing care from the very first moment of arrival.

headings.title: Operation Bed
headings.content: An operation bed, commonly referred to as an anesthetic, recovery, or postoperative bed, is specially arranged to receive a patient returning from the operating theater. The overarching priority in making an operation bed is to facilitate the safe, rapid, and effortless transfer of an unconscious or semi-conscious patient from a stretcher, while keeping them warm, secure, and easily accessible for post-anesthesia monitoring. The top covers—comprising the sheet, blanket, and spread—are folded back completely to one side of the bed or fan-folded lengthwise to the edge opposite the doorway or stretcher approach. This leaves the bed wide open for transfer. To maintain body temperature, which is often compromised due to anesthesia and cool operating room environments, thermal aids such as hot water bottles (used with strict caution and protective covers to prevent burns) or warming blankets are placed on the bed prior to the patient's arrival and removed before they are positioned. A rubber or plastic draw sheet covered with a cotton draw sheet is placed under the head and trunk area to protect the mattress from vomitus, blood, or wound drainage. Additionally, an emesis basin, tissues, suction tubing, and an oxygen setup should be readily available at the bedside to manage potential postoperative complications like aspiration or respiratory depression.

headings.title: Cardiac Bed
headings.content: The cardiac bed is a specialized bed arrangement designed to provide maximum comfort and respiratory support for patients experiencing acute cardiac conditions, severe congestive heart failure, or profound respiratory distress such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). When a patient suffers from orthopnea—the inability to breathe comfortably while lying flat—standard bed positioning exacerbates their dyspnea. The cardiac bed addresses this by utilizing a high Fowler's position supported by an arrangement of multiple pillows behind the back and head, and crucially, placing a specialized cardiac table (or over-bed table with a pillow) across the front of the patient. This setup allows the patient to lean forward slightly, which fixes the shoulder girdle and engages the accessory muscles of respiration to improve lung expansion and oxygenation. A soft pillow or folded sheet is often placed under the knees to prevent hyperextension and reduce pressure on the popliteal blood vessels, preventing venous stasis and deep vein thrombosis. Foot boards may also be utilized to prevent foot drop. Nurses must frequently assess the patient's respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and skin integrity over bony prominences when maintaining a cardiac bed configuration.

headings.title: Patient Safety, Comfort, and Ergonomics
headings.content: Patient safety, comfort, and ergonomic principles are core pillars of professional nursing practice during any bed-making procedure. Safety measures include locking the bed wheels before starting the procedure to prevent accidental rolling, raising the bed to a comfortable working height to prevent nurse fatigue and injury, and ensuring side rails are appropriately managed according to the patient's clinical status. Comfort is achieved by ensuring that the mattress is supportive, the linens are tightly stretched and wrinkle-free to avoid skin irritation, and crumbs or foreign objects are brushed away before remaking. Ergonomics involves applying correct body mechanics—such as keeping the nurse's feet wide apart for a stable base of support, bending at the knees rather than the waist, and using body weight to push or pull heavy loads. In busy Nigerian wards where nursing staff frequently manage heavy workloads, mastering ergonomics prevents chronic occupational back pain and burnout. Additionally, involving or reassuring the patient throughout the process maintains their dignity and emotional well-being, completing the standard of comprehensive, patient-centered care.
